solution.concept_anchor: Ashokan pillar edict site-content pairs

statement_analysis.statement: The Allahabad (Prayagraj) pillar bears the Major Pillar Edicts I–VI as well as the Schism Edict and the Queen's Edict.
statement_analysis.reason: The Allahabad pillar carries Major Pillar Edicts I–VI and the Queen's Edict (recording Queen Karuvaki's donations) but does NOT carry the Schism Edict. The Schism Edict is found at Sarnath, Sanchi, and Kausambi.

statement_analysis.statement: The Delhi-Topra pillar, originally erected at Topra (Haryana) and moved to Delhi by Firuz Shah Tughlaq, carries Pillar Edict VII — the only pillar to carry all seven Major Pillar Edicts.
statement_analysis.reason: Delhi-Topra (Firozabad column) is the only Ashokan pillar bearing all seven Major Pillar Edicts; the Delhi-Meerut pillar carries only Edicts I–VI. This makes Delhi-Topra uniquely significant in Ashokan epigraphy.

statement_analysis.statement: The Sarnath pillar bears the Schism Edict warning against divisions in the Buddhist Sangha, in addition to carrying Major Pillar Edicts.
statement_analysis.reason: The Sarnath pillar carries the Schism Edict but does NOT carry the full series of Major Pillar Edicts — these two edict types appear on separate pillars. The Sarnath pillar is specifically noted for the Schism Edict and the famous lion capital.

statement_analysis.statement: Firuz Shah Tughlaq transported two Ashokan pillars to Delhi — one from Topra (Haryana) and another from Meerut (Uttar Pradesh).
statement_analysis.reason: Historical records confirm Firuz Shah Tughlaq had two Ashokan pillars transported to Delhi: the Topra pillar (now at Firozabad/Delhi) and the Meerut pillar (Delhi-Meerut), both documented in his reign.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Only two correct) is also the answer, but students may miscount by accepting Statement 1 (assuming Allahabad has the Schism Edict since it has many edicts) and rejecting Statement 4 (unsure about Firuz Shah's specific actions).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: The Allahabad pillar has Major Pillar Edicts I–VI and the Queen's Edict — NOT the Schism Edict. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Statement 2: Delhi-Topra is the only pillar with all seven Major Pillar Edicts — a well-documented fact. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 3: Sarnath carries the Schism Edict but not the full Major Pillar Edict series — the two sets appear on different pillars. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statement 4: Firuz Shah Tughlaq moved two pillars — from Topra and Meerut — to Delhi. Statement 4 is correct.
Two statements (2 and 4) are correct — select option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in Statement 1 exploits the fact that the Allahabad pillar is the most famous individual Ashokan pillar (it also carries Samudragupta's inscription), leading students to assume it carries the maximum number of edict types including the Schism Edict. The Schism Edict's three locations (Sarnath, Sanchi, Kausambi) must be memorised precisely; Allahabad is not among them.
solution.final_explanation:
The distribution of specific edict types across Ashokan pillars is a precision-recall topic frequently tested in UPSC.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Allahabad (Prayagraj) pillar carries Major Pillar Edicts I–VI and the Queen's Edict. The Schism Edict is NOT on the Allahabad pillar — it is found at Sarnath, Sanchi, and Kausambi.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Delhi-Topra pillar (Topra, Haryana; moved to Delhi by Firuz Shah Tughlaq) is uniquely the only Ashokan pillar bearing all seven Major Pillar Edicts, including Pillar Edict VII which deals with dhamma as a comprehensive social ethic.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Sarnath pillar carries the Schism Edict — true. But the claim that it ALSO carries Major Pillar Edicts is incorrect; the two bodies of edicts appear on separate pillars.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Firuz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351–1388 CE) transported two Ashokan pillars to Delhi — the Topra pillar and the Meerut pillar — a well-documented act of antiquarian interest by a medieval sultan.

Value Addition:
• The Delhi-Meerut pillar carries only Edicts I–VI (missing Edict VII), making Delhi-Topra uniquely complete.
• Firuz Shah Tughlaq wrote about moving the pillars in his autobiography Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi.
• The Queen's Edict on the Allahabad pillar names Queen Karuvaki and records her donation of mangoes, gardens, and money to Buddhist institutions.

solution.concept_anchor: Yaksha-yakshi tradition — folk origin predating Mauryan court art
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion A correct? Yes. Yaksha-yakshi figures in the Mauryan period — like the Didarganj Yakshi and Parkham Yaksha — are characterised by robust, voluminous forms with frontal posture, monumental scale, and simplified but powerful modelling — this is an accepted stylistic description.

Step 2 — Is Reason R correct? No. Yaksha-yakshi worship is rooted in pre-Buddhist indigenous fertility and nature-deity cults, not in the Vedic yajnic (sacrificial) tradition. Yaksha figures are associated with nature worship, tree spirits, and wealth — not Vedic sacrificial ritual. R incorrectly attributes their origin to the Vedic yajnic tradition.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer is option c regardless of the causal relationship.
A is correct, R is incorrect — select option c.
solution.final_explanation:
Yaksha-yakshi sculptures represent the robust popular art tradition that ran parallel to the refined court art of the Mauryan period. They embody indigenous folk religious sensibilities — nature worship, fertility cults, and tree-deity veneration.

Assertion (A) — Correct: Mauryan-period yaksha-yakshi figures are indeed characterised by a distinctive visual vocabulary: imposing monumental scale, robust and voluminous corporeal forms, rigid frontal stance (samabhanga posture), and schematised but powerful modelling of faces and bodies. Examples include the Didarganj Yakshi and Parkham Yaksha.

Reason (R) — Incorrect: Yaksha-yakshi worship does NOT originate from the Vedic yajnic (sacrificial) tradition. Yakshas and Yakshinis are part of a pre-Vedic or para-Vedic stratum of Indian religious belief — associated with nature spirits, tree deities, water bodies, and fertility. They were gradually absorbed into both Buddhist and Hindu traditions but their cultic roots are in folk animism, not Vedic sacrifice.

Value Addition:
• Buddhism assimilated yaksha-yakshi figures as guardians of sacred sites — they appear on Sanchi and Bharhut toranas as protectors.
• The Kubera (god of wealth) connection to yakshas demonstrates their association with prosperity rather than Vedic ritual sacrifice.
• Yakshinis are among the earliest representations of the female form in Indian art — predecessors of the later apsaras and river goddesses of temple architecture.

solution.concept_anchor: Stupa sites matched with state and distinguishing feature
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because it correctly pairs Sanchi with Madhya Pradesh (which students know) but mismatches Piprahwa and Amaravati, tempting students who know one or two pairs confidently but guess the others.
elimination_logic: Sanchi: definitively in Madhya Pradesh — most important Buddhist monument complex (A–2).
Piprahwa: in Uttar Pradesh (Siddharth Nagar district, near Kapilavastu) — stupa with relic casket inscription (B–4).
Amaravati: in Andhra Pradesh (Guntur district) — great Satavahana-period stupa known for its distinctive sculptural style (C–1).
Lauriya Nandangarh: in Bihar (West Champaran) — Ashokan pillar with lion capital AND a large stupa (D–3). Correct: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 — option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap involves Piprahwa, which many students loosely associate with Nepal (because it is near the Nepal border and linked to Kapilavastu, the Buddha's hometown) rather than precisely identifying it as being in Uttar Pradesh, India. Similarly, Amaravati students may confuse with Maharashtra (because Satavahanas also operated there) rather than Andhra Pradesh. These geographic precision traps distinguish prepared from partially prepared students.
solution.final_explanation:
The geographic distribution of major stupa sites spans multiple states and is a recurring UPSC geography-culture crossover topic.

Correct pairings:
• A–2: Sanchi — Madhya Pradesh. The most comprehensively preserved Buddhist monument complex in India, featuring the Great Stupa and its famous toranas.
• B–4: Piprahwa — Uttar Pradesh (Siddharth Nagar district). Contains an early stupa with a relic casket bearing one of the oldest Brahmi inscriptions, identifying Buddha's relics.
• C–1: Amaravati — Andhra Pradesh (Guntur district). The great Satavahana-period stupa known for its distinctive sculptural style (Amaravati School) featuring elaborate narrative limestone panels.
• D–3: Lauriya Nandangarh — Bihar (West Champaran). The site of an Ashokan pillar with a lion capital and a large associated earth stupa — often paired with nearby Lauriya Araraj.

Value Addition:
• Amaravati stupa sculptures are now partly in the British Museum (London) and the Chennai Government Museum.
• Piprahwa's proximity to Kapilavastu (the Buddha's hometown) makes it one of the most pilgrimage-significant sites in the Buddhist world.
• The Amaravati School's distinctive style — elongated figures, dynamic narrative compositions — influenced Southeast Asian Buddhist art directly.

solution.concept_anchor: Sanchi monument chronological sequence — Mauryan to Satavahana
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c places the Shunga stone casing after the torana construction, which students unfamiliar with Sanchi's precise construction sequence might accept since they associate the famous carved gateways with 'later' additions without knowing the exact sequence.
elimination_logic: Original Mauryan brick stupa (Ashoka period, c. 250 BCE) is the foundational layer — must come first.
Shunga period enlargement and stone casing (c. 150–100 BCE) came next — the brick stupa was doubled in diameter and given a stone outer casing.
The stone vedika (railing) was added around the same time as or slightly after the Shunga casing — but before the toranas.

Toranas (gateways) were the last major additions — carved during the early Satavahana period (c. 1st century BCE to 1st century CE). Correct order: Mauryan brick stupa → Shunga enlargement/stone casing → Vedika → Toranas — option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap involves the relative ordering of Shunga stone casing and torana construction. Many students know that 'the toranas were added later' and 'Ashoka built the stupa' but cannot precisely place the Shunga enlargement between these two events. Placing the toranas before the stone casing (option c) is the most common sequence error — students assume the gateways and the enclosure were part of the same Shunga-period campaign.
solution.final_explanation:
The Sanchi Great Stupa (Stupa 1) is a layered monument built over several centuries, with each major addition reflecting a different patronage period.

Correct chronological sequence:
1. Mauryan brick stupa (c. 250 BCE): Ashoka commissioned the original stupa — a relatively modest brick structure.
2. Shunga period enlargement and stone casing (c. 150–100 BCE): Shunga rulers oversaw a major expansion — the stupa was enlarged to its current diameter and encased in stone, with a medhi (terrace) added for elevated pradakshina.
3. Stone vedika (railing) addition: The outer enclosure wall (vedika) of stone was added roughly contemporaneously with the Shunga casing.
4. Toranas (gateways) (c. 1st century BCE – 1st century CE): The four elaborately carved gateways — the iconic feature of Sanchi — were the last major additions, constructed during the early Satavahana period with donations from guilds and lay Buddhists.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option a would place toranas before Shunga casing — incorrect.
• Option c reverses the casing and torana sequence — the most common error.
• Option d would place the Mauryan construction after Shunga work — impossible.

Value Addition:
• Torana inscriptions name individual donors — ivory workers from Vidisha, for instance — providing evidence of guild patronage.
• UNESCO inscribed Sanchi in 1989 recognising 'living testimony to the development of Buddhism over several centuries.'
• Stupa 2 at Sanchi (on a lower terrace) predates the toranas of Stupa 1 and contains a simpler railing without figural carving.

solution.concept_anchor: Megasthenes vs Fa-Hien accounts — contemporaneous vs retrospective testimony
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because students who recall that Fa-Hien visited India and described Buddhist sites may assume his palace account is equally reliable as primary evidence, not recognising the 600-year gap between Fa-Hien's visit and Ashoka's reign.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: The researcher should not accept Megasthenes and Fa-Hien as equivalent primary sources — they are separated by approximately 600 years and represent very different types of testimony.

Eliminate option b: Fa-Hien's account (5th century CE) is retrospective — he visited approximately 600 years after Ashoka; his description reflects Buddhist hagiographic tradition about Ashoka, not direct observation of an intact palace.

Eliminate option c: Dismissing Megasthenes entirely is unwarranted — while he may have exaggerated, he was a contemporary ambassador at Chandragupta's court and provides the closest eyewitness account available.

Confirm option d: The correct approach is to privilege Megasthenes as a near-contemporaneous observer over Fa-Hien as a retrospective religious commentator, while cross-checking both against Kumrahar archaeological evidence — which confirms large-scale palatial construction but does not confirm all textual claims.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap in option b presents Fa-Hien as equally reliable primary evidence. Students unfamiliar with the temporal gap between Fa-Hien (5th century CE) and Ashoka (3rd century BCE) may assume both foreign accounts carry equal evidential weight. Fa-Hien's account of the palace is hagiographic — reflecting how the palace was remembered in Buddhist tradition centuries after it was built — not a direct observation like Megasthenes' near-contemporaneous description.
solution.final_explanation:
A researcher studying the Mauryan palace at Pataliputra must evaluate multiple types of evidence — contemporaneous literary accounts, retrospective foreign accounts, and physical archaeological remains.

Applicable principle: In historical methodology, contemporaneous sources carry greater evidential weight than retrospective accounts; both must be cross-checked against material evidence.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Treating Megasthenes and Fa-Hien as equivalent primary sources ignores a ~600-year temporal gap. They represent fundamentally different types of testimony.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Fa-Hien visited in the early 5th century CE — approximately 600 years after Ashoka's reign. His account of the palace reflects Buddhist hagiographic tradition ('built by supernatural beings') not direct observation. Using it as primary contemporaneous evidence is methodologically unsound.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Dismissing Megasthenes entirely is excessive — he was a Seleucid ambassador at Chandragupta Maurya's court, making him the closest to a contemporaneous observer of the palace. His account, while possibly exaggerated, provides the most temporally proximate literary testimony.
• Option (d): Correct. The sound methodology is to weight Megasthenes more heavily as near-contemporaneous testimony, treat Fa-Hien as retrospective hagiographic tradition, and use the Kumrahar archaeological evidence (sandstone pillar bases of the 80-pillar hall) as the controlling material check on both accounts.

Value Addition:
• Megasthenes' Indica survives only in fragments quoted by later Greek and Roman authors (Strabo, Arrian, Diodorus).
• Fa-Hien's account of Pataliputra also describes the city's charitable institutions — hospitals and rest houses — providing evidence of Gupta-period urban governance.
• The 80-pillar hall at Kumrahar may be the 'Apadana' described by Megasthenes — but this identification remains debated.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

(b) Use Fa-Hien's account as the more reliable primary source since it was written more recently in historical time and reflects accumulated Buddhist tradition about the palace
(c) Dismiss Megasthenes' account as Greek exaggeration and rely exclusively on the Kumrahar archaeological findings
(d) Treat Megasthenes as near-contemporaneous testimony and Fa-Hien as retrospective hagiographic tradition, using Kumrahar material evidence to cross-check both accounts

solution.concept_anchor: Rampurva bull capital — location in Rashtrapati Bhavan
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Sarnath Lion Capital — Indian Museum, Kolkata) is a strong distractor because students may confuse where the Sarnath capital is currently housed, with many associating 'Indian Museum' with Mauryan artifacts.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: The Sarnath Lion Capital is in the Sarnath Archaeological Museum (near Varanasi) — not in Delhi.
Evaluate option b: The Sarnath Lion Capital is housed in the Sarnath site museum — NOT the Indian Museum, Kolkata (which houses Bharhut railings). Option b is incorrectly matched.
Evaluate option c: The Rampurva Bull capital is indeed displayed in the Rashtrapati Bhavan, New Delhi — this is a well-documented fact. Option c is correctly matched.
Eliminate option d: The Didarganj Yakshi is in the Patna Museum — not the National Museum, New Delhi. Option c is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap works on multiple levels: the Indian Museum (Kolkata) is associated with major Mauryan finds (Bharhut railings), making option b plausible. Students who know that Kolkata's Indian Museum houses important ancient Indian sculptures may assign the Sarnath capital to it. The Sarnath capital's actual location — the site museum at Sarnath itself — is a less prominent fact that distinguishes precise from approximate knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
The current museum locations of major Mauryan artifacts are a recurring precision-recall topic in UPSC.

• Option (a): Sarnath Lion Capital — National Museum, Delhi: Incorrect. The Sarnath Lion Capital is housed in the Sarnath Archaeological Museum (also known as the Sarnath Site Museum), Uttar Pradesh — not in Delhi.
• Option (b): Sarnath Lion Capital — Indian Museum, Kolkata: Incorrect. The Indian Museum, Kolkata, houses the Bharhut stupa railings (Shunga period) — not the Sarnath capital.
• Option (c): Rampurva Bull Capital — Rashtrapati Bhavan, New Delhi: Correct. The Rampurva bull capital (from Bihar) is displayed in the Rashtrapati Bhavan complex, making it one of the few Mauryan-period artworks in a constitutional building.
• Option (d): Didarganj Yakshi — National Museum, Delhi: Incorrect. The Didarganj Yakshi is in the Patna Museum (Bihar Museum complex), Patna — not the National Museum.

Value Addition:
• The Bharhut railing pillars in the Indian Museum, Kolkata, are some of the most important Shunga-period narrative sculptures.
• The Sarnath site museum also houses other sculptures found at Sarnath, including Gupta-period Buddha images.
• The Patna Museum (now the Bihar Museum) houses a significant collection of Mauryan-period artifacts from the Patna region.

solution.concept_anchor: Court art decline vs folk art continuity — post-Mauryan transition

statement_analysis.statement: The Mauryan court art tradition — characterised by monolithic polished pillars and palatial stone-working — effectively disappeared after the decline of the Mauryan empire, while the popular folk art tradition continued and flourished under subsequent dynasties.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the standard art-historical assessment: Mauryan polish and monolithic pillar-making did not survive the empire's fall, while popular Buddhist art (stupa decoration, yaksha-yakshi tradition) continued vigorously into the Shunga, Satavahana, and later periods.

statement_analysis.statement: The post-Mauryan flourishing of popular folk artistic traditions, such as the elaborately carved Sanchi toranas, was made possible primarily because royal Shunga patronage actively promoted folk artistic themes over the courtly artistic vocabulary of the Mauryan period.
statement_analysis.reason: The Sanchi toranas and similar post-Mauryan Buddhist sculpture were sustained primarily by guild and merchant patronage (documented in torana donor inscriptions), not by royal Shunga promotion of folk themes over courtly vocabulary. The Shungas did patronise Sanchi but the attribution of the folk-art flourishing to deliberate royal promotion of folk over court styles is an unsupported causal claim.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) is deceptive because Statement 1 is clearly correct, and Statement 2's narrative about Shunga patronage has a grain of truth (Shunga rulers did patronise Sanchi) that masks the false causal attribution.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Court art decline + folk art continuation is the standard accepted framework. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The Sanchi toranas were funded primarily by guilds and merchants (documented in inscriptions), not by royal Shunga decree to promote folk over court styles. This reversed-causation claim attributes the folk-art flourishing to a royal agenda that is not supported by evidence. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap in Statement 2 inverts the actual dynamic: it was the withdrawal of imperial patronage (not deliberate royal promotion of folk art) that allowed guild and merchant patronage to fill the vacuum and drive the folk-art tradition forward. Students who know 'Shunga rulers patronised Buddhist monuments' may accept the causal story in Statement 2 without noticing that it misidentifies the mechanism — the patronage was opportunistic and economic (guild/merchant donations), not a deliberate royal aesthetic programme.
solution.final_explanation:
The transition from Mauryan to post-Mauryan art represents one of Indian art history's great paradoxes: the end of imperial patronage did not diminish Buddhist art but transformed its patronage base and intensified its narrative richness.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The technical traditions specific to Mauryan court art (monolithic polished pillars, palatial stone architecture) were not transmitted to successor dynasties. Meanwhile, the popular Buddhist artistic tradition — stupa construction, narrative carving, yakshi figures — entered a creative golden age under Shunga and Satavahana contexts.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The post-Mauryan flourishing of popular Buddhist art was driven by guild and merchant patronage, as evidenced by donor inscriptions on Sanchi toranas naming craftsmen, merchants, and even dancing girls as donors. The Shunga rulers did patronise Sanchi, but the folk-art flourishing cannot be attributed to a royal programme of promoting folk over court vocabulary — that claim reverses the actual causation (institutional patronage shift) into a false intentional narrative.

Value Addition:
• The shift from royal to mercantile patronage reflects the growing economic power of trading guilds (shrenis) in post-Mauryan India.
• Sanchi torana inscriptions are a primary source for understanding non-royal artistic patronage in ancient India.
• The Bharhut stupa railing (Shunga period) similarly shows extensive evidence of donor inscriptions from non-royal sources.

solution.concept_anchor: Achaemenid vs Mauryan pillar — key structural difference
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because Achaemenid pillars at Persepolis do have elaborate capital decorations and students who recall 'Persian influence on Mauryan art' may assume the decorative programme was also adopted from Persia, including the monolithic-versus-sectional distinction.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option b: The presence of elaborate capital decorations is common to both Achaemenid and Mauryan traditions — this is not the key structural difference.
Eliminate option c: Both traditions used stone — this is not the distinguishing feature.

Eliminate option d: Inscriptions are a distinctive Mauryan feature, but the question asks about the most fundamental structural/technical difference — and inscriptions are not a structural construction feature.

Confirm option a: The most fundamental technical difference is that Mauryan pillars were carved from a single piece of stone (monolithic), while Achaemenid pillars at Persepolis were assembled from multiple stone drums — this is the defining structural distinction cited in art history literature.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges stylistic influence with structural identity: students who know 'Persian influence on Mauryan pillars' may assume the structural technique was also borrowed, not realising that the monolithic single-piece construction is precisely what sets Ashokan pillars apart FROM their Persian counterparts. The stylistic borrowing (bell capitals, animal friezes) did not extend to the Achaemenid multi-drum construction method — Mauryan craftsmen independently achieved the technically more demanding monolithic carving.
solution.final_explanation:
The comparison between Ashokan and Achaemenid pillars is a standard examination topic that requires distinguishing aesthetic borrowing from structural independence.

• Option (a): Correct. Ashokan pillars were monolithic — carved from a single block of Chunar sandstone. Achaemenid pillars at Persepolis were constructed from multiple stone drums stacked vertically. This structural difference is the most fundamental technical distinction.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Elaborate capital decorations appear in both traditions — this is not a distinguishing feature.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Both traditions used stone; this is a shared feature, not a differentiating one.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Inscriptions are distinctive to Ashokan pillars (Achaemenid pillars at Persepolis bear no comparable edict-type inscriptions), but inscriptions are not a structural/construction technique feature — the question asks about the construction distinction.

Value Addition:
• The monolithic carving of pillars weighing up to 50 tonnes and transporting them hundreds of kilometres is one of ancient India's most impressive engineering achievements.
• Chunar quarries (near Varanasi) supplied the stone; evidence of ancient quarrying activity has been found there.
• The multi-drum Achaemenid construction technique was more modular and replaceable — the monolithic Mauryan approach was technically more ambitious.

solution.concept_anchor: Stupa component functions — harmika, medhi, vedika distinctions

statement_analysis.statement: The medhi in stupa architecture refers to the raised circular terrace at the base of the anda that provides an elevated pradakshina path, distinct from the ground-level circumambulatory path.
statement_analysis.reason: The medhi is the raised platform or terrace encircling the base of the anda; it allows circumambulation at an elevated level and is structurally separate from the ground-level circumambulatory path around the vedika.

statement_analysis.statement: The vedika (railing) around a stupa served an exclusively decorative function, with no role in demarcating sacred from profane space.
statement_analysis.reason: The vedika served both a symbolic and a functional role: it demarcated the sacred Buddhist monument space from the surrounding secular world — a boundary marker with deep ritual significance, not merely a decorative element.

statement_analysis.statement: The harmika atop a stupa's anda symbolically represents a heavenly palace or sacred enclosure from which the chattravali (parasol stack) rises as a royal-divine emblem.
statement_analysis.reason: The harmika is interpreted as a celestial palace or sacred fence enclosing the relic deposit below; the chattravali rising from it symbolises the Buddha's royal-divine status — a tiered parasol being the marker of sovereignty.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) tempts students who accept Statements 1 and 3 without critically examining Statement 2's 'exclusively decorative' qualifier.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Medhi as raised terrace for elevated circumambulation — standard stupa anatomy. Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: 'Exclusively decorative' with 'no role in demarcating sacred space' — the vedika's primary function is sacred boundary demarcation, not decoration. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: Harmika as heavenly palace + chattravali as royal emblem — accepted symbolic interpretation. Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 2 works by including a true element (the vedika is visually prominent and often elaborately carved, hence 'decorative') while attaching a false absolute claim ('exclusively decorative' and 'no role in demarcating sacred space'). Students who recall that Bharhut and Sanchi railings are carved with elaborate decorative scenes may focus on the decorative aspect and miss the fundamental ritual boundary-marking function of the vedika.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding stupa component terminology and their symbolic functions is essential for both descriptive and analytical questions on Mauryan and Buddhist architecture.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The medhi is the raised circular terrace encircling the stupa base, providing an elevated circumambulatory path. At Sanchi Stupa 1, the medhi allows pradakshina at a height above the ground-level path around the outer vedika.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The vedika's primary function is the demarcation of sacred (Buddhist monument) space from secular surroundings — it is a ritual boundary. While vedika panels at Bharhut and Sanchi are elaborately carved (making them visually decorative), calling their function 'exclusively decorative' ignores their fundamental role as sacred enclosure markers.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The harmika, a small square railing atop the anda dome, represents a heavenly palace or divine enclosure — the Buddha's residence in a symbolic cosmological sense. The chattravali (stacked umbrellas) rising from it signifies the Buddha's royal-divine sovereignty.

Value Addition:
• Early Buddhist texts describe the stupa as a 'body of the Buddha' — each structural element corresponds to a part of the body.
• The number of tiers in the chattravali varies and carries symbolic meaning — more tiers indicating greater sanctity of the enshrined relic.
• Vedika inscriptions at Bharhut and Sanchi are among the earliest sources for personal names, occupations, and family relationships in ancient India.
